desc:
Return true if there are three indices i < j < k such that nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k] (strictly increasing values), otherwise return false. The indices do not have to be adjacent.

Examples: [2, 1, 5, 0, 4, 6] is true (for instance 1, 4, 6); [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] is false. Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
hints: Trying all triples is O(n<sup>3</sup>). Think about what you need to remember while scanning left to right.
Keep the smallest value seen so far (a) and the smallest value that already has a smaller value before it (b), i.e. the best end of an increasing pair.
For each x: if x ≤ a set a = x; else if x ≤ b set b = x; otherwise x is larger than a pair end, so return true.
editorial: We maintain the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length 1 (a) and of length 2 (b). A new value that does not exceed a lowers a; one that exceeds a but not b lowers b; one that exceeds b completes a triple. This is the length-3 special case of the patience-sorting tails array used for the longest increasing subsequence.

A subtle point: when a is lowered after b was set, the old pair behind b is still valid, because a smaller a appearing later does not erase the earlier pair that justified b. Only the existence of some earlier smaller element is needed, not its identity.
